title: Small-world networks yield tunable quantum codes at short circuit depth
abstract: Monitored random quantum circuits naturally generate quantum error-correcting codes. We generate quantum codes with tunable properties by implementing random Clifford circuits on Watts--Strogatz `small-world' networks and tailor code properties via three knobs: nonlocal graph rewiring, measurement rate, and circuit depth. On fully rewired networks, circuits of logarithmic depth produce codes with a finite rate and an extensive mean contiguous distance with failure probability substantially lower than codes produced from local circuits. These small-world codes form at a circuit depth growing as $\ln n$ compared to polynomial depths required for codes produced from local networks. Rewiring also moves the purification transition to higher measurement rates and changes its critical exponents. Connectivity is thus a knob for designing codes.

bite.hook: Small-world random quantum circuits produce quantum codes at logarithmic depth ln n instead of polynomial depths.
tldr: Generated quantum error-correcting codes using random Clifford circuits on Watts-Strogatz small-world networks.
Varied three knobs: nonlocal graph rewiring, measurement rate, and circuit depth.
Found that logarithmic depth produces codes with a finite rate and low failure probability compared to local circuits.
bite.whyItMatters: Building fault-tolerant quantum computers requires efficient quantum error-correcting codes. Showing that network connectivity can act as a design knob opens new, faster pathways to generate these vital codes.
bite.eli5: Imagine trying to send a secret message across a group of friends. If everyone only talks to their immediate neighbors, information travels very slowly. But if a few long-distance phone lines are added—a small-world network—messages zip across instantly, helping build sturdy quantum error-codes much faster.
